Chapter Two: Replacing False Beliefs with Truth and Building a New Self-Image.
Now that you've started to recognize those deeper roots of pain, let's talk about the next step—taking a look at the beliefs that have grown from those wounds.
You know, so many of us end up living with a set of assumptions about ourselves and about the world—assumptions we picked up during some of our most vulnerable moments.
And, most of the time, these beliefs just slip quietly into the background, shaping our choices and relationships without us even noticing.
False beliefs can show up in all sorts of ways.
Maybe you’ve caught yourself thinking you’re not lovable, or that your mistakes are all that people see.
Sometimes it feels like happiness is always just out of reach.
Or, maybe you’ve felt like God is distant or hard to please, which makes it tough to trust in kindness or unconditional love.
These kinds of beliefs are like tinted glasses—we end up seeing every experience through that lens, and it really limits what we think is possible.
Healing, deep down, is about finding these false beliefs and choosing to replace them with the truth.
It’s not a quick fix.
Think of it more like a journey, a gradual process of renewal that starts with awareness.
It’s about catching those moments when negative self-talk or old assumptions pop up.
Like, maybe you notice the thought, “I always mess things up,” and instead of letting it slide, you pause and ask yourself—Is that really true?
Here’s a metaphor that might help: beliefs are like the operating system of your mind.
If your system’s running on old, buggy code, you’re going to keep getting the same errors.
But you can update that system—by intentionally installing new, healthier beliefs.
So, how do you actually do that?
Let’s walk through a few practical steps:
First, start by noticing your negative self-talk.
Pay attention to that inner dialogue, especially when you’re stressed or disappointed.
Next, challenge those old assumptions.
Ask yourself if a belief is really accurate, or if it’s just something you picked up from past pain rather than what’s true for you now.
Then, try affirming new truths.
Use statements that reflect a kinder, more compassionate view—not just of yourself, but of how loved you really are.
And finally, surround yourself with supportive voices.
That could be people, books, podcasts—anything that helps reinforce the positive beliefs you’re working to build.
One thing I want you to really hold onto is this: your self-worth isn’t something you have to earn.
From a place of faith, you’re seen as valuable and deeply loved, no matter what your past looks like or what you’re going through right now.
Embracing that truth can change everything—it’s the starting point for dissolving shame and fear.
Picture this: someone grows up feeling invisible in their family.
Over time, they start to believe their needs just don’t matter.
As an adult, that belief shows up as difficulty setting boundaries or speaking up.
But, by recognizing where that belief came from, and practicing new ways of thinking—like reminding themselves, “My voice matters”—the old pattern can finally start to shift.
This isn’t about ignoring pain or pretending everything’s perfect.
It’s about bringing real compassion, and real truth, to the places where old wounds have shaped who you are.
And, little by little, as new beliefs take root, you’ll notice your soul becoming stronger, more open to joy, and ready to move forward with greater confidence.
